findings.claim: five of his brothers and sisters died in infancy
findings.truth: Five brothers, not brothers and sisters. Pip reads five stone lozenges beside his parents' grave.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 1: 'To five little stone lozenges... sacred to the memory of five little brothers of mine'

findings.claim: she raises Pip 'by hand,' ... it literally means she breastfed him (hand-rearing)
findings.truth: Reversed. 'Brought up by hand' means reared WITHOUT the breast - fed by hand with a spoon or bottle. Dickens's joke is that Pip takes it to mean Mrs Joe's heavy hand.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 2 'brought up by hand'; standard Victorian usage

findings.claim: He tells Pip: 'We'd be uncommon. We'd go down the river and see the ships.'
findings.truth: Fabricated. Joe never says this. No 'see the ships' line belongs to Joe; the only such phrase (ch. 46) describes Bill Barley's bow-window.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg full-text search for 'uncommon', 'oncommon', 'ships' returns no such line. Replaced with ch. 7: 'Ever the best of friends; an't us, Pip? Don't cry, old chap!'

findings.claim: Miss Havisham raises Estella to be 'proud and hard and beautiful' (also lesson 6 content and both flashcards)
findings.truth: The phrase is not in the novel. Miss Havisham's own words are 'proud and hard' (ch. 38).
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 38: 'Estella, Estella, Estella, to be proud and hard to me!' No match for 'hard and beautiful'

findings.claim: Miss Havisham ... dies in agony, consumed by the fire that engulfs her wedding dress
findings.truth: Pip smothers the fire and saves her (ch. 49). She lingers, and Joe reports she died about a week after Pip fell ill (ch. 57).
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 49 rescue passage; ch. 57: 'Arter you was took ill, pretty much about what you might call... a week'

findings.claim: He cries in the garden: 'I took the opportunity of being alone to use my sleeve to wipe my eyes.'
findings.truth: Fabricated - welded from two separate ch. 8 sentences. Pip cries behind a gate in the brewery-lane.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 8: 'leaned my sleeve against the wall there, and leaned my forehead on it and cried. As I cried, I kicked the wall, and took a hard twist at my hair'

findings.claim: he went home and kicked the wall of the forge in frustration
findings.truth: He kicks the brewery wall at Satis House immediately after Estella leaves, not the forge wall at home.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 8, same passage as F6

findings.claim: He looks at Joe's honest, soot-covered face and feels 'a growing dissatisfaction' with his home.
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. The real line is ch. 15, after a Satis House visit and BEFORE the news of the expectations.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 15: 'I felt more than ever dissatisfied with my home and with my trade and with everything'. Ch. 18 has only 'dissatisfied with myself'

findings.claim: He describes Magwitch's hands as 'coarsened and hardened'; exam tip tells students to quote 'coarsened', 'hardened'
findings.truth: Neither word appears in the novel. Ch. 39 gives 'large brown veinous hands' and 'The abhorrence in which I held the man, the dread I had of him, the repugnance with which I shrank from him'.

findings.claim: Miss Havisham, whose wealth derived from her family's brewery and Compeyson's fraud
findings.truth: Reversed. Compeyson defrauded HER: he 'got great sums of money from her' and made her buy out her brother's brewery share at an immense price.

findings.claim: Compeyson received a lighter sentence because he 'looked like a gentleman' while Magwitch, 'in rags and dirt,' was sentenced to fourteen years
findings.truth: Both quoted phrases are invented. The real ch. 42 wording is Magwitch's, and the sentences were seven years for Compeyson and fourteen for Magwitch.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 42: 'how gentlemanly Compeyson looked, wi' his curly hair and his black clothes and his white pocket-handkercher, and what a common sort of a wretch I looked'; 'ain't it him as gets seven year, and me fourteen'

findings.claim: In Chapter 44, he tells her: 'You let me go on' - accusing her
findings.truth: Speaker error. Pip asks 'at least you led me on?'; 'I let you go on' is Miss Havisham's reply, an admission not an accusation.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 44: 'Yes,' she returned, again nodding steadily, 'I let you go on.'

findings.claim: Pip, Herbert, and a boatman attempt to smuggle Magwitch out of England
findings.truth: No boatman. Wemmick tells Pip specifically not to hire a Thames waterman - 'Take Startop.' Startop rows with Pip and Herbert.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 45: 'know a better course than taking a Thames waterman. Take Startop.'; ch. 54 rowing party

findings.claim: Miss Havisham - he jilted her at the altar.
findings.truth: She never reached the altar. Compeyson's letter arrived while she was dressing, at twenty minutes to nine.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 22: 'The day came, but not the bridegroom. He wrote her a letter'

findings.claim: The adult narrator comments with devastating simplicity: 'Joe had brought with him a simple dignity.'
findings.truth: Misquoted and misplaced. The real line, 'I had not been mistaken in my fancy that there was a simple dignity in him', ends Joe's LONDON visit (ch. 27), not the nursing scene (ch. 57).
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 27 line 9455; ch. 57 line 19473 'O Joe, you break my heart!'

findings.claim: Pip takes her hand and says: 'I saw no shadow of another parting from her.'
findings.truth: The line is narration in the past tense, not speech to Estella.

findings.claim: He wants to prove that even a convict can 'make' a gentleman: 'Own colonist as shall be a gentleman!'
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. The real boast is: 'All on you owns stock and land; which on you owns a brought-up London gentleman?'

findings.claim: Practice question 6: 'Compare the two endings Dickens wrote for Great Expectations. Which is more effective and why? [30 marks]', labelled '30 marks - 19th Century Essay' with an AO1/AO2/AO3 mark scheme.
findings.truth: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B always prints an extract and asks 'Starting with this extract, how does Dickens present...'. A compare-the-two-endings evaluation is never set, so the AQA mark scheme attached to it misleads. Options: (a) reword as an extract-anchored question on the final chapter and keep the mark scheme, or (b) relabel it as a discussion task, not a 30-mark exam question. Recommend (a).
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, Specification at a glance, Paper 1 Section B

findings.claim: 'He calls the knaves, Jacks, this boy!' (lessons 1, 7) and 'Ever the best of friends, ain't us, Pip?' (lessons 6, 7)
findings.truth: Punctuation and dialect variants only. Gutenberg #1400 reads 'He calls the knaves Jacks, this boy!' (no comma after knaves) and 'an't us, Pip?'. Both site spellings occur in printed school editions; no mark impact, so left alone.

summary: All 7 lessons carry at least one finding; the dominant failure mode is fabricated or misattributed quotation (7 HIGH), not exam-claim error. Every exam claim checks out against AQA 8702: 30 marks, AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6, extract printed, no SPaG on Section B, and no Shakespeare mislabelling anywhere in the unit.
